intro: After a hushed night scene, one girl is chosen to dance herself to death. Stravinsky conducts a final dance of short, savage chords, with plucked cellos and basses sharpening the blows.

sections.label: Intro · Night before the sacrifice
sections.mNote: Soft wind chords and divided strings

sections.label: A · Mystic Circles of the Young Girls
sections.mNote: Six solo violas begin the circling tune

sections.label: B · Glorification of the Chosen One
sections.mNote: Eleven chords announce the chosen victim

sections.label: C · Evocation of the Ancestors
sections.mNote: Low brass calls; high winds answer

sections.label: D · Ritual Action of the Ancestors
sections.mNote: Cor anglais sings over horns, plucked strings and drums

sections.label: E · Sacrificial Dance
sections.mNote: Short chords, plucked basses and sudden gaps

cues.title: Night in the orchestra
cues.text: Flutes and clarinets murmur soft repeated chords while the oboes hold long notes. Horns and muted trumpets add their voices; divided strings spread the sound further. The marking is Largo. After the first part’s pounding finish, this slow opening seems to find the dancers standing in darkness.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 86–88, rehearsal figures 79–80, Introduction to Part II: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. The ballet scenario places the second part at night: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The elders wear bearskins
cues.text: Nicholas Roerich’s imagined ancient world gives the elders bearskins and gathers the girls into a circle. One girl will remain in the middle. The elders wait for her last dance: the whole ceremony narrows down to a single body.
cues.evidence: Roerich and Stravinsky’s scenario, including the elders in bearskins and the chosen girl’s death, is reproduced in the K catalogue: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring. Van den Toorn, chapter 1, discusses their collaboration and the invented sacrificial rite: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

cues.title: Six violas in a circle
cues.text: Six solo violas carry the melody together, each on a different note. Two solo cellos add high harmonics. Stravinsky asks the violas to sing warmly without getting loud; the girls’ circling begins with a tenderness that the coming choice will destroy.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 96, rehearsal figure 91, Andante con moto; six solo viola parts marked molto cantabile ma non forte, with two solo cellos in harmonics: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A toothache in Clarens
cues.text: On 17 November 1912, Stravinsky writes in his sketchbook at the Châtelard Hotel in Clarens: “with an unbearable toothache I finished the music of the Sacre”. The grand ritual has a very ordinary witness: a composer who needs a dentist.
cues.evidence: Stravinsky’s sketchbook, p. 97, dated 4/17 November 1912; the quoted English translation appears in Van den Toorn, chapter 2, with the Clarens and Châtelard Hotel inscription: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

cues.title: Eleven blows choose her
cues.text: Eleven repeated chords interrupt the circling. Strings, timpani and bass drum strike together. Then Vivo releases a fast dance whose bars keep changing length. The chosen girl stands at the centre while the others acclaim her fate.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 101–02, rehearsal figures 103–104: eleven repeated chords precede the Glorification, which opens with changing 5/8 and 9/8 bars: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. The scenario identifies this dance as the glorification of the selected victim: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The ancestors are summoned
cues.text: Bass clarinets and low brass begin the invocation; high winds and brass answer with hard, repeated chords. The phrases are blunt and short. This summons has no room for the circling melody’s gentleness.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 115–18, rehearsal figures 121–128, Evocation of the Ancestors: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A cor anglais prayer
cues.text: Horns, plucked strings and soft percussion set out a quiet repeating figure. Above it, the cor anglais curls through a small, plaintive phrase. The accompaniment keeps going beneath the solo, as patient and implacable as the elders around the girl.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 119–21, rehearsal figures 129–131, Ritual Action of the Ancestors; the cor anglais enters over repeated horn, pizzicato-string and percussion figures: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Paris carries the composer
cues.text: On 5 April 1914, Pierre Monteux conducts The Rite of Spring at the Casino de Paris. This time it is a concert. Admirers carry Stravinsky on their shoulders afterwards, less than a year after the uproar at the ballet’s premiere.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 1, p. 6, recounts the 5 April 1914 concert under Monteux and Stravinsky’s being carried on the shoulders of admirers: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

cues.title: Chords cut into silence
cues.text: The last dance begins in short, sharp chords. Cellos and basses pluck underneath them, making each blow bite. Rests split the gestures apart; the next chord arrives before the body can settle into an easy pattern of steps.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, pp. 39–41, describes the opening of the 1943 Sacrificial Dance and its pizzicato cellos and basses, rehearsal figures 1–9 in that edition: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html. The K catalogue identifies the revised finale in this January 1960 performance: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The composer rewrites the dance
cues.text: In 1943, Stravinsky rewrites the final dance’s bars, note values and scoring. Much of the notation doubles in size: quavers become crotchets. This 1960 performance uses that revision, giving the orchestra a later set of instructions for the girl’s ordeal.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 2, pp. 39–54, documents the 1943 revision, including the doubled note values: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html. The K catalogue specifies this text for the recording made on 5–6 January 1960: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring

transitions.title: Six violas start the circle
transitions.to: A · Mystic Circles of the Young Girls
transitions.how: The introduction’s low horn phrases subside. At Andante con moto, six solo violas begin a harmonised melody, with high cello harmonics around it and low strings beneath. The violas are marked molto cantabile ma non forte: full of song, still quiet. The circle starts to turn.

transitions.title: Eleven chords break the circle
transitions.from: A · Mystic Circles of the Young Girls
transitions.to: B · Glorification of the Chosen One
transitions.how: Climbing runs lead into eleven hammering chords in strings, timpani and bass drum. The other winds and brass fall silent for these blows. Then Vivo begins the Glorification, with short orchestral bursts and changing bar lengths. The girl has been chosen; the music gives her no time to answer.

transitions.title: A pause before the summons
transitions.from: B · Glorification of the Chosen One
transitions.how: A general pause separates the Glorification from the summons. Bass clarinets and low brass enter over held low strings; brighter wind and brass chords answer them. The new crotchet takes the speed of the preceding dotted quaver, keeping a small pulse alive across the silence while the phrases grow broader.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 114–15, rehearsal figures 120–121, including the general pause and dotted-quaver-to-crotchet tempo equation: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf

transitions.title: The cor anglais takes up the rite
transitions.to: D · Ritual Action of the Ancestors
transitions.how: The invocation slows to Lento, with descending bassoon figures. The Ritual Action settles into a quiet accompaniment of low horns, plucked strings and percussion. A cor anglais melody rises over it. The busy summons has brought the elders into place; their ceremony can proceed at a measured tread.

transitions.title: The last dance cuts in
transitions.from: D · Ritual Action of the Ancestors
transitions.how: Winding clarinet and bass-clarinet phrases fade over the ritual’s quiet low accompaniment. The final dance cuts in with short orchestral chords, sharpened by plucked cellos and basses. Changing bar lengths and abrupt rests break up the blows. The girl’s solo begins on a floor that will not hold still.
transitions.evidence: The closing Ritual Action is shown in the full score, p. 128, rehearsal figures 140–141: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. For the different 1943 finale used here, Van den Toorn, pp. 39–41, documents the opening chords and pizzicato low strings: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html. Recording version: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: He could make a roomful of dancers lose their footing with one displaced accent, then write a psalm that scarcely moves.
facts: Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes · Ramuz’s travelling theatre · Balanchine · Auden and Kallman
Ballets, operas, symphonies and sacred music; composing and recording into his eighties
composer.background:
In St Petersburg, opera was the family business. Stravinsky’s father, Fyodor, sang bass at the Mariinsky Theatre; Igor heard him on stage and began piano lessons at nine. Born in 1882 at Oranienbaum, he entered St Petersburg University to study law. There he befriended Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, whose father heard his first pieces in 1902. Rimsky-Korsakov took him on privately, giving regular lessons from 1905 until his death in 1908. The pupil orchestrated pages of Pan Voyevoda, then had to explain why his teacher had scored them differently.

He married his cousin Catherine Nossenko in 1906; by 1914 they had four children. His E♭ Symphony owed much to Glazunov and Tchaikovsky; Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks showed what he could do with an orchestra in a few minutes. Sergei Diaghilev heard his music in 1909 and gave him some Chopin to orchestrate for Les Sylphides. Then came a whole ballet, The Firebird. Stravinsky handed over the score in sections while Michel Fokine worked out the dances. In his 1936 autobiography he remembered the rehearsals ending with dinner beside Diaghilev and Nijinsky, and good claret.
